title: Exact Shannon capacity of odd cycles and small graphs
short_statement: Determine the Shannon capacity of basic graphs such as odd cycles beyond $C_5$, especially $C_7$, and clarify the computational complexity of the graph capacity invariant.
full_statement: For a finite graph $G$, let $G^{\boxtimes k}$ denote the $k$-fold strong product of $G$ with itself, and let $\alpha(H)$ be the independence number of a graph $H$. The Shannon capacity of $G$ is $$\Theta(G)=\sup_{k\ge 1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}.$$ Equivalently, $G$ is a confusability graph for a zero-error communication channel, and $\Theta(G)$ is the asymptotic number of distinguishable symbols per channel use. The open problem is to compute or tightly characterize $\Theta(G)$ for fundamental graph families and to determine the computational complexity of approximating or deciding bounds on $\Theta(G)$. A concrete benchmark is the odd cycle $C_7$: determine the exact value of $\Theta(C_7)$, or even close the best upper and lower bounds enough to reveal the correct structural mechanism. A broader resolution would explain whether Shannon capacity admits effective approximation algorithms, semidefinite/asymptotic-spectrum certificates, or inherent noncomputability-like finite-prefix barriers.
open_problem: Compute $\Theta(C_7)$ and, more generally, determine the algorithmic complexity and approximability of graph Shannon capacity.
background: Shannon introduced zero-error capacity to capture communication when the receiver must decode with no possibility of confusion. Translating a channel to its confusability graph gives a beautiful combinatorial invariant: independent sets in strong powers of the graph are zero-error codes. The model is exceptionally clean, but the invariant is hard because it is asymptotic over all powers of the graph. Lovasz's solution for the pentagon $C_5$ via the theta function is one of the classic successes of semidefinite optimization in combinatorics; it also highlights the mystery, because the same machinery does not settle even the next odd cycles. The problem belongs on ORdos because it is a crisp optimization limit, tied to SDP bounds, asymptotic spectra, and finite-object certificate search.
known_results: Shannon defined the capacity invariant and solved several elementary cases. Lovasz introduced the theta number and proved $\Theta(C_5)=\sqrt 5$, giving an efficiently computable semidefinite upper bound that is tight for perfect graphs and some special nonperfect graphs. Haemers introduced rank-based upper bounds that can beat Lovasz theta on some graphs, and later work developed Schrijver, fractional, projective-rank, and asymptotic-spectrum tools. For odd cycles beyond $C_5$, exact capacities remain unknown. Computational and constructive work has improved lower bounds for $C_7$, $C_{11}$, $C_{13}$, $C_{15}$ and related graphs by finding large independent sets in graph powers. Alon and Lubetzky showed that the sequence $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})$ can have complicated behavior, so no fixed finite prefix of powers can generally approximate capacity within subpolynomial factors. Recent asymptotic-spectrum and graph-limit work provides new language and some improved bounds, but the basic small-instance benchmark $\Theta(C_7)$ remains unresolved. The 2026 construction sequence includes Buys-Polak-Zuiddam's July preprint bound $\Theta(C_7)\ge3.258805369885\ldots$, a later repository update to $3.258827985920\ldots$, and Tandon's August preprint Theorem 2 giving $\Theta(C_7)\ge3.258832620353\ldots$ from an explicit independent set in $C_7^{\boxtimes500}$. The Lovasz upper bound is $7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\approx3.317667$. These are lower-bound improvements, not exact capacity.

where_posed.text: The open status of small odd cycles and the finite-prefix obstruction are discussed in Shannon-capacity papers and surveys; Alon and Lubetzky give a formal obstruction to finite-prefix approximation.

counterexample_rationale: Lower-bound progress is often an explicit independent set in a finite strong power. Such objects are finite certificates and can be verified exactly by graph computation.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search and evolutionary methods can hunt for large independent sets in graph powers, discover symmetry-reduced constructions, and test SDP/rank upper-bound candidates. Exact upper bounds remain much harder but can sometimes be certified by SDP dual solutions or algebraic arguments.

literature.synthesis: The capacity problem has two faces. For a fixed graph such as $C_7$, progress can come from finite combinatorial objects: larger independent sets in $C_7^{\boxtimes k}$ improve lower bounds, while theta/rank/asymptotic-spectrum methods improve upper bounds. For the general computational problem, Alon and Lubetzky show why naive finite-prefix extrapolation cannot work: the independence numbers of powers can behave too irregularly. Recent asymptotic-spectrum work reframes capacity as part of a broader theory of asymptotic invariants, but has not eliminated the gap on the standard odd-cycle benchmarks. A solution for $C_7$ would likely reveal a new certificate type, either a surprisingly structured code or a sharper universal upper-bound method. The recent recursive constructions improve the finite-power lower bounds; their reported exact-arithmetic and Lean certificates were not rerun in this audit.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For lower bounds, search for independent sets in strong powers of odd cycles using symmetry, SAT/IP formulations, coding-theoretic ansatzes, and local improvement. For upper bounds, study Lovasz-theta strengthenings, Haemers-rank variants over fields, asymptotic-spectrum elements, and dual SDP certificates. Keep separate the fixed-graph problem, such as $C_7$, from the general complexity question.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A lower-bound submission should provide the graph, power $k$, and an explicit independent set; a referee can verify pairwise nonadjacency in $G^{\boxtimes k}$ and compute the implied $\alpha^{1/k}$ bound. An upper-bound claim must give a valid capacity upper bound, not merely a bound on one finite independence number. If the proof uses theta or another SDP, provide a dual certificate or interval-certified numerical solution. For complexity claims, distinguish exact computation, additive approximation, multiplicative approximation, and promises on the input graph family.
